opus-5.5.text:
I think it's worth separating two questions that often get blurred together: what pretrained encoders give you for *understanding* the scene and the task, and what they give you for *acting* in it.

On the understanding side, the value is pretty clear. If you want a robot to respond to "pick up the red mug next to the laptop," you really don't want to learn the concepts of "mug," "red," and "laptop" from your own robot data. You'll never collect enough of it. Language and vision models trained on internet-scale data already have those concepts, so you inherit a lot of semantic generalization for free: new objects, new phrasings, new environments that look different from your training set. That's where we've seen the biggest gains.

Where I'm more cautious is the assumption that these representations transfer directly to control. A lot of vision encoders are trained to be invariant to exactly the things a policy cares about. For a classification objective, it doesn't matter whether the cup is two centimeters to the left. For a grasp or a footstep, that's the whole problem. So you often see that a frozen pretrained backbone gives you good semantics but mediocre spatial precision, and you either need to fine-tune it, combine it with geometric inputs like depth or proprioception, or add some structure that preserves fine-grained spatial information.

Coming from the locomotion side, I'd add that a lot of what makes a robot robust isn't semantic at all. It's contact dynamics, timing, reacting to a slip in milliseconds. Pretrained encoders don't really help there. That knowledge comes from physics, either through simulation and reinforcement learning or through real interaction data. So the picture I find most convincing is layered: use large pretrained models for the high-level "what and where," and use policies trained with lots of embodied experience, often in simulation, for the low-level "how."

In terms of how to actually assess the value, I'd push for evaluations that deliberately separate those axes. Test semantic generalization with novel objects and instructions, test physical generalization with new terrains, payloads, and disturbances, and see which component is responsible for which gains. Otherwise it's easy to credit the pretrained encoder for robustness that really came from the data or the training setup, or to blame it for failures that are really about control.

r002.rationale: It discusses spatial precision and control transfer, but does not say small lighting-induced embedding changes can cause a policy to fail.

r003.rationale: It recommends separating evaluation axes, but does not state that the overall generalization benefits remain to be demonstrated.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure, so that's a question I get asked a lot, and I think my answer is a bit more nuanced than people expect, because most of my work has been on the low-level control side — locomotion, whole-body control, things trained in simulation with reinforcement learning — and there, honestly, pretrained encoders haven't played a huge role yet.

If you look at a locomotion policy, the inputs are proprioception, maybe a height map or a depth image, and the output is joint targets at fifty hertz or so. The thing that policy needs to understand is contact, dynamics, how the body responds to actions. A vision encoder trained on internet images doesn't really know anything about that. So for that layer of the stack, I'd say the value is pretty limited, and in practice we end up training small encoders from scratch in sim because they're fast, they're tailored to the sensor, and they don't introduce latency that we can't afford on the real robot.

Where I think it becomes genuinely valuable is one level up, when you start asking the robot to do something semantically meaningful — go to the kitchen, pick up the red object, follow this person. There, the generalization you want is not about dynamics, it's about recognizing the world, and that's exactly what these models are good at. You get a notion of objects and language for free that you'd never get from simulation data alone, because our simulators are great at physics and pretty bad at the visual diversity of the real world.

So the way I tend to think about it is as a division of labor. The pretrained models give you a semantic understanding of the scene and a language interface, and the RL-trained low-level controller gives you a robust, physically grounded skill that you can call into. The interface between them is where a lot of the interesting design questions are right now. How much do you let the high-level model influence the low-level behavior? Do you pass through a latent, a set of commands, waypoints? We've experimented with giving the controller a fairly rich command space, so the high level can shape the motion without needing to understand contact dynamics.

The other caveat I'd add is that it's easy to overestimate how much generalization you're actually getting. A frozen encoder can look great in a demo and then fail because the features it produces aren't tuned to what matters for control — fine-grained geometry, relative positions, timing. So we often find some fine-tuning or at least a learned adapter is needed, and then you're back to the question of how much real data you have.

So, to sum up: I think they're very valuable for perception and semantics, modest value for control itself, and the real progress is going to come from figuring out how these two worlds plug into each other cleanly.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very promising, but it’s useful to separate generalization in perception from generalization in control. A pretrained vision encoder might recognize an object in an environment the robot has never seen. A language encoder might help connect different descriptions of a task. Those are valuable capabilities, and learning all of that from robot interaction alone would be very expensive.

But recognizing an object doesn’t necessarily tell you how to manipulate it. You still need to connect those representations to actions and to the consequences of those actions. Two objects can look very similar but have different physical properties, so the policy may need to interact with them to figure out what to do.

The question for me is how much of that pretrained knowledge actually transfers into successful behavior. If we change the objects, the background, or the task, does the robot still succeed? That’s where these encoders could make a big difference, but I wouldn’t assume that broad visual or language understanding automatically gives you a broadly capable robot policy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very useful, but it depends on what kind of generalization you’re looking for. A pretrained vision encoder can give you features that are much more robust to changes in appearance than something you train only on your robot data. And language gives you a way to describe tasks and share information across them.

But understanding what’s in an image, or understanding an instruction, doesn’t automatically tell the robot how to act. You still need to learn that connection to the robot’s observations and actions. So I would distinguish semantic generalization—recognizing a new object or interpreting a new instruction—from generalizing the physical skill needed to interact with it.

The interesting question is how much of that pretrained representation actually transfers to control. I’d want to test it on new objects, environments, and tasks, and compare it with simpler representations. These encoders are a promising starting point, but they don’t remove the need for good robot data and a policy that can learn from it.
